name: Carlos Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Carlos, thanks for sitting down with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the regional supermarket chain, the branch in the old mill town down the valley. Early mornings I'm in goods-in at the back, unloading the lorry and checking the delivery against the sheet, and then I'm on tills or on the floor till two. I'm still the new one in the stockroom, I mix up the pallets sometimes and the older guy, Ray, has to sort me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lorry mornings, it's physical, you feel like you've done something by eight. I don't love the till, people can be rude when the card machine is slow. Tough part is the pay, it's the bottom of the scale, and there's not much else in the valley since the mill closed.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, she's the receptionist at the primary school. On Saturdays I help my uncle with his small roofing business, carrying tiles, mostly. I use AI apps once in a while, Ana showed me how to use one for writing a letter to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Makes sense to me, a lot of things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool like any other, use it if it helps and don't if it doesn't. At work we'd carry on unloading lorries. I'm not really an online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I'm still on the bottom rate in a town with not many jobs. We've got less than a month of money saved, and the car needs new tyres. Nothing's on fire, but nothing's getting better either unless I make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager about the shift supervisor training, because the company does have a scheme for it. I'd keep doing Saturdays with my uncle, it's an extra eighty most weeks. And I'd try to put that eighty away instead of spending it on the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I want more than this, but I'm not going to whinge about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the supervisor scheme involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's six months, a few hours a week on top of shifts, learning rotas and stock and handling complaints. If you pass you get a small raise. Ray says I should go for it, even though I'm still slow on pallets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should fix low pay in the valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Businesses, by growing, not the government handing things out. If more firms opened here, they'd compete for workers and pay would go up. My job is to make myself worth more.

At work we'd just **carry on** unloading lorries.
think: I'm still on the **bottom rate** in a town with few jobs.
We've got **under a month** saved and the car needs tyres.
do: Apply for the company's **shift supervisor** scheme.
Keep doing **Saturdays** roofing with his uncle for about eighty a week.
Save the eighty instead of spending it **at the pub**.
S0.quote: My job is to make myself worth more.
fieldNote: Believes pay rises come from **business growth**, not government.
Steady about change and keen on a **supervisor scheme** his colleague Ray recommends.
Thin savings and a car needing **tyres** keep him on edge.

steps.text: Apply for the company's six-month shift supervisor scheme
Keep working Saturdays for his uncle's roofing business
Save the Saturday roofing money instead of spending it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, writing and booking and answering. Ana's job is basically that, the school phone and the forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress goes, and people who adapt will be fine. At work I'd say the stockroom's safe for a while. To family I'd say we'll manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm more worried about Ana than me. The school office is all emails and booking and answering parents, which is exactly what this card says. My lorry mornings are hands-on, so I've got some years, but if her hours drop we're short on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the supervisor scheme, but I'd learn the rota software and the ordering system properly, because that's where the AI shows up first. I'd ask my uncle if he'd take me on as a roofing apprentice, properly, with a qualification. And I'd tell Ana to ask the school about teaching assistant training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious. I don't like not knowing what Ana's job looks like in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who adapt will be fine. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. But I've seen what happened when the mill closed, and not everyone landed on their feet. My dad never really worked again properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your uncle feel about taking you on properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be glad, I think, he's got no sons in the business. But he'd want me committed, not doing it part-time while I keep the shop. That's a big step on a thin cushion.

The **stockroom** is safe for a while.
think: **Ana's school office** job is exactly the work this card describes.

Urge Ana to ask about **teaching assistant** training.
feel: **Anxious** about not knowing what **Ana's job** looks like.
S1.quote: I've seen what happened when the mill closed, and not everyone landed on their feet.
fieldNote: Quickly sees his girlfriend's **receptionist** job as more exposed than his own.
His public faith in **adapting** is tempered by his father's experience after the mill.
A real **roofing apprenticeship** with his uncle is on the table.

steps.text: Learn the store's rota and ordering software on the scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AGI, then robots by 2031. That's a lot faster than I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have to stand on their own feet, but also that companies can't just drop everyone overnight. At work there'd be a lot of nervous jokes. I'd tell my mates to get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Ana's school office job goes almost straight away. My goods-in job lasts till the robots, maybe 2031, and the planning side changes even sooner. So we'd have three years where I'm the main earner on bottom pay, and that doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time with my uncle as a roofing apprentice right away, even though it's less money at first, because robots on roofs feel a long way off. Ana would look for teaching assistant or care work, something with kids or people. We'd sell the second-hand car and use the bus to save on insurance and fuel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. Losing work to robots would be like the mill closing again, but faster and for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say don't wait for anyone to save you, that's what he learned. He'd also say get a trade, which he always says. For once I'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said selling the car. How would you get to the roofing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle picks me up anyway, he drives past the flat. Ana can walk to the school. It'd be tight, but the car costs us nearly two hundred a month.

say: People must stand on their **own feet**, but companies can't drop everyone **overnight**.
I'd tell my mates to **get a trade**.
think: **Ana's office** job goes almost straight away.

fieldNote: Expects his girlfriend's income to go **within two years**, which drives his alarm.
Echoes his father: **don't wait** to be rescued, get a trade.
Would **sell the car**, a big step in a valley town with few jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots 2034. That's still quick, but you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort yourself out if you're not lazy about it. At work I'd tell the younger lads to take the apprenticeships while they're there. I'd keep politics out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have till 2034 in goods-in, seven years, and Ana's office changes around 2031. That's enough time to get my roofing qualification part-time. It's tight, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time roofing apprenticeship with my uncle next spring, keeping two shifts at the supermarket for steady money. Ana would do teaching assistant training at the college in the evenings. We'd put the wedding talk on hold until one of us has a proper trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but focused. More like before a match than before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put the wedding on hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to be able to look after a family properly first. That's how I was raised. Ana says I'm old-fashioned, but she agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in roofing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for quotes and measuring from photos, my uncle hates paperwork. If it's proven to work, I'd try it. I'm not going to be the first, but I won't be the last.

I'd tell younger lads at work to **take apprenticeships**.

Ana's school **office** changes around 2031, before my job does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with this much warning, for anyone. People should use the time to get a skill. I'd say companies should invest in training, but it's their call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd be okay. Ten years is a full roofing qualification and a few years running jobs. The supermarket's still going to need fewer of us, so I'd want out before 2035 anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor scheme now and start the roofing apprenticeship within two years. I'd try to save three months of money by 2028, so we can get married and maybe think about a deposit. Ana would retrain as a teaching assistant before her office changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly calm. The usual worry about money doesn't go away though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your life to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, maybe a kid, working with my uncle or running the roofing business when he retires. Ana in a classroom. A small house in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could knock that off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, a bad winter for roofing, or the car dying. Small things knock you off when you've got nothing saved. That's the real enemy, not the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ana's job goes first and mine soon after, and we've got nothing behind us. What would help is apprenticeships that pay enough to live on, and businesses opening in the valley again. I don't want a handout, I want a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about towns like ours. The mill closing taught us that a whole valley can lose its work at once. If robots do the same, it's not just jobs, it's the pubs and the football club and everything.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a trade.
portrait: Carlos is 27, working **goods-in** and tills at a chain supermarket in a valley **mill town**.
He lives with **Ana**, a school receptionist whose job is more exposed to AI than his.
He helps his uncle's **roofing** business on Saturdays and sees a trade as his route.
He believes in standing on his **own feet**, shaped by his father's struggle after the mill closed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Ana's job goes first and his soon after with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships that pay **enough to live** on, and new **businesses** in the valley.
